REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES DEPARTMENT OF THE mTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT Francisco Gold Condominium II, EDSA cor. Mapagmahal St., Diliman, Quezon City OF THE UNDERSEQETARY FOR LOCAL , s. NO 44 S. 16 June 2008 Am. ROGELIO U. MARASIGAN ATIY. PIO KENNETH 1. DASAL Law Department City Hall, Makati City Qenuemen: This has reference to your earlier letter seeking our legal opinion on whether your Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) City Federation President can sign a Contract of Service in behalf of the SK City Federation considering that she Is still a minor. In reply thereto, may we respectfully point out that "capacity to act" has been defined under Article 37 of the New Civil Code as the power to do acts with legal effect. When RA 6809 has lowered the age of majority In the Philippines from twentyone (21) to eighteen (18) years old, those who reached the age of 18 years are now given the full capacity to act. Corollarily, under Article 38 of the same Code, It is provided that "minority" Is a mere restriction on one's capacity to act. It being a restriction, it is erroneous to say that a minor has no capacity to act. Hence, a minor has a capacity to act but the same is restricted. For instance, under the CMI Code of the Philippines, a minor is allowed to enter into a contract provided that there is parental consent. As a general rule, therefore, minors have restricted capacity to act. The case, however, is different with respect to the capacity to act by SK officials with respect to certain matters.

-2- In this regard, may we note that under Sections 426 and 430 of the Local Qovemment Code, the Sangguniang Kabataan as a colleØaI body, and the SK Chairmen, respecdvely, were conferred by law with certain powers, duties and funcdons. These provisions contained the express grant of such powers and the mandate to perform certain duties and functions. At this point, It Is not even amiss to point out that the SK Chairmen and officials may be held liable and accountable for their failure to perform these duties, functions and powers. The Local Qovemment Code, particularly Section 456 thereof, likewise provided for the creation of the SK federations and mandated them to exercise certain powers in the federation In accordance with the Constitution and By Laws of the SK and the Local Qovemment Code. Along this line, it becomes imperative for us to discuss the doctrine of "necessary implication". This doctrine Is explained, thus: "No statute can be enacted that can provide au the details involved in its application. There is always an omission that may not meet a particular situation. What is thought, at the time of enactment, to be an an-embracing legislation may be inadequate to provide for the unfolding Of ewnts of the fiature. So-caned gaps in the taw develop as the taw is enforced. One of the rules of statutory construction used to in the gap is the doctrine of necessary implication. The doctrine states that what is implied in a statute is as much a part thereof as that which is expressed. Every statute is understood, by implication, to contain att such provisions as may be necessary to effectuate Its object and purpose, or to make effectiw rights, powers, privileges or jurisdiction which it grants, Including au such collateral and subsidiary consequences as may be fairly and logically inferred from its terms. Ex necessitate legis. And every Statutory grant of power, right or privilege is deemed to Include au incidental power, right or privilege. This is so because the greater includes the lesser, expressed in the maxim, in CQ plus sit, inest minus." (Chua vs. Civit Service Commission, G.R. No. 88979, 07 February 1982, as cited in the case of Atienza vs. Villarosa, G.R. No. 161081, IO May 2005). By applying the aforesaid doctrine, it can be certainly said that the express conferment of such powers, duties and functions to the SK Chairmen and officials would also include the Implied conferment of capacity to act unto the SK officials, thus, empowering them to do certain

-3- acts with legal effect in order for them to effectively and efficiently discharge and carry out their statutorily mandated powers, duties and functions. A contrary view would render meaningless the powers, dudes and functions lodged by law to these SK officials. In addidon, It bears to that the Local Qovemment Code is a later law dealing specifically on local govemment units and its officials while the New Civil Code Is a prior law, which Is a general law. Applying the rules on statutory construction, the specific provisions in the Local Government Code granting certain powers to SK officials can be considered to have modified Articles 37 and 38 of the New Civil Code of the Philippines. Moreover, laws are presumed to have been passed with full knowledge of all exisdng laws on the subject (U.S. vs. Palacio, 33 Phil. 308). Foregoing considered, it can be fairly concluded that while SK officials are minors and thus, generally with restricted capacity to act, the restriction, however, will not apply to SK officials insofar as to matters relating to the exercise of thelr mandated dudes, powers and functions under the Local Qovemment Code and other existing laws are concemed since in the discharge thereof, their acts should be given legal effect. Obviously, however, as to other matters, the restriction by reason of minority still applies. Hence, we so hold that the SK City Federation President can sign Contracts of Services in behalf of the City SK Federation. Hope we have enlightened you on the matter. Very truly yours, AUSTERE A.
